title: Cantor 1874: Algebraic Numbers Are Countable — The Theorem That Created Transcendental Number Theory
content:
This module formalizes Cantor's 1874 theorem that the algebraic numbers are countable. The result appears in the same paper ('Über eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen') where Cantor proved the real numbers are uncountable — the first demonstration that infinite sets can have different sizes.

The historical significance is profound:
- Before 1874: mathematicians knew of no transcendental numbers (numbers that are not roots of any rational polynomial)
- Hermite 1873: proved e is transcendental — the first specific transcendental
- Cantor 1874: proved 'almost all' reals are transcendental (in the sense of cardinality), before anyone knew how to construct them
- Liouville 1844 had earlier shown transcendental numbers exist by explicit construction (Liouville's constant), but Cantor's cardinality argument showed they must be 'everywhere'

The formalization proves 18 theorems organized in 7 sections: direct results (delegating to Mathlib), bounded-degree sets, exact-degree stratification, degree union decomposition, degree 1 = rationals, cardinality equality, and exhaustive filtration. Two proof styles are used: the direct one-line delegation to `Algebraic.countable`, and the constructive degree-stratification proof via `Set.countable_iUnion`.
mathContext: Countability hierarchy for number systems: ℕ ≅ ℤ ≅ ℚ ≅ algebraic reals (all ℵ₀) ⊊ ℝ ≅ ℂ ≅ transcendental reals (all 2^ℵ₀). The key fact: |{degree ≤ d polynomials over ℚ}| = |ℚ^{d+1}| = ℵ₀, and each polynomial has ≤ d roots. So |{algebraic reals of degree ≤ d}| ≤ d · ℵ₀ = ℵ₀. The union over d ∈ ℕ remains ℵ₀.

title: algebraic_reals_countable: One-Line Proof via Mathlib's Algebraic.countable
content:
The shortest proof in the file is the most fundamental:

```lean
theorem algebraic_reals_countable : Set.Countable {x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} :=
  Algebraic.countable ℚ ℝ
```

`Algebraic.countable` (in `Mathlib.Algebra.AlgebraicCard`) proves: if R is a countable commutative ring and E is an R-algebra, then the set of R-algebraic elements of E is countable. Applied with R = ℚ (which is countable/Denumerable) and E = ℝ, this gives the result in one line.

The cardinality strengthening `card_algebraic_reals_eq_aleph0` uses `Algebraic.cardinalMk_of_countable_of_charZero ℚ ℝ`, which needs char(ℝ) = 0 (characteristic zero). This condition ensures infinitely many distinct algebraic numbers exist (ruling out the finite case). The result Cardinal.mk {...} = Cardinal.aleph0 is strictly stronger than Set.Countable — it proves countably infinite, not just countable.

Both real and complex cases are handled: `algebraic_complex_countable` and `card_algebraic_complex_eq_aleph0` use ℂ instead of ℝ, and `Algebraic.countable ℚ ℂ` works because ℂ is also a ℚ-algebra.
mathContext: Mathlib's `Algebraic.countable` proof works as follows: algebraic elements of E over R are a subset of roots of all nonzero polynomials in R[X]. There are countably many such polynomials (R[X] is countable when R is countable), each has finitely many roots. The countable union of finite sets is countable. This is exactly the degree-stratification argument, packaged abstractly.

title: Two Stratification Levels: Bounded vs Exact Degree — A Filtration Structure
content:
The formalization defines two nested families of sets:

**Bounded degree**: `algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d = {x | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ natDegree(minpoly x) ≤ d}`
- Forms a monotone chain: deg≤0 ⊆ deg≤1 ⊆ deg≤2 ⊆ ...
- Union equals all algebraic reals (proven in §7)
- `bounded_degree_monotone`: monotonicity proved by Nat.le_succ_of_le

**Exact degree**: `algebraicRealsOfDegree d = {x | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ natDegree(minpoly x) = d}`
- Each a distinct, disjoint horizontal slice
- `exact_degree_subset_bounded`: degree d ⊆ bounded degree d (le_of_eq converts = to ≤)
- Union equals all algebraic reals (proven in §4)

The relationship: algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d = ⋃_{k≤d} algebraicRealsOfDegree k. Both are countable (as subsets of the countable set of all algebraic numbers via Set.Countable.mono).

Countability of bounded-degree sets is proved first (§2), then exact-degree (§3) uses it as an intermediate step via the inclusion chain: exact d ⊆ bounded d ⊆ all algebraic (countable).
mathContext: The bounded-degree filtration is an algebraic analogue of truncated Taylor series: algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d can be thought of as 'numbers algebraically describable by polynomials of complexity ≤ d'. As d → ∞, this exhausts all algebraic numbers. This is formalized in `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_bounded`.

title: Degree Stratification: algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree and the Alternative Countability Proof
content:
The degree stratification theorem `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree` proves:
{x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} = ⋃ d : ℕ, algebraicRealsOfDegree d

The proof is a `by ext x; simp; constructor` argument:
- **(→)**: Given IsAlgebraic ℚ x, take d = (minpoly ℚ x).natDegree. Then x ∈ algebraicRealsOfDegree d since natDegree(minpoly ℚ x) = d by rfl.
- **(←)**: Given ⟨d, hx, _⟩, extract IsAlgebraic from hx.1 (the first component of the conjunction defining algebraicRealsOfDegree).

`algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata` then uses this to give an alternative proof:
```lean
rw [algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree]
exact Set.countable_iUnion algebraicRealsOfDegree_countable
```

`Set.countable_iUnion` proves: if I is a countable index type (ℕ is Countable) and each A i is countable, then ⋃ i, A i is countable. Applied with A d = algebraicRealsOfDegree d (each countable by algebraicRealsOfDegree_countable), this gives the result.
mathContext: The key lemma `Set.countable_iUnion` requires the index type to be countable (ℕ satisfies this). Without this condition, the union of countably many countable sets could be uncountable (the union of uncountably many countable sets is not necessarily countable). The degree index is ℕ — a countable well-order — which makes this valid.

title: One Theorem, Two Proofs: algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata as a Methodological Exhibit
content:
The four lines of `algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata` are not new mathematics — the theorem statement is **identical** to `algebraic_reals_countable` proved in §1. What is new is the *route*. The original (§1) is a one-line delegation to `Algebraic.countable ℚ ℝ`, treating Mathlib's general theorem as a black box. This alternative re-derives the same result from the degree stratification:

```lean
theorem algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata :
    Set.Countable {x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} := by
  rw [algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree]
  exact Set.countable_iUnion algebraicRealsOfDegree_countable
```

The pedagogical lesson: in formal mathematics, having *two independent proofs* of the same theorem is itself a result. It exposes the internal structure of the algebraic numbers (a countable union of countable strata indexed by degree), and it confirms that Mathlib's abstract `Algebraic.countable` is consistent with the constructive degree-by-degree count that Cantor used in 1874. Removing either proof would lose information: §1 gives the shortest road to a usable lemma; §4 gives the route a student or another formalization could re-walk from first principles.

Note: `algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata` is technically redundant in the formal sense — its conclusion equals an already-proved theorem — but every formalization library values such redundant proofs for exactly this exposition-of-structure reason. Mathlib itself ships many `_via_*` lemmas for the same purpose.
mathContext: The two proofs realise the dichotomy between **set-theoretic** (\S 1: ${\rm Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \{x \mid \text{IsAlgebraic } \mathbb{Q}\ x\}$ is countable by Mathlib's general statement) and **combinatorial** (\S 4: ${\rm Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \bigcup_{d \in \mathbb{N}} \text{alg}_d$, a countable union of countable strata). The latter is exactly Cantor's 1874 argument unpacked: enumerate by degree, then by polynomial within each degree. Both proofs ultimately rely on the same Mathlib fact $|\mathbb{Q}[X]| = \aleph_0$, but \S 4 surfaces this dependence through the degree filtration whereas \S 1 hides it inside $\texttt{Algebraic.countable}$.

title: Degree 1 = Rationals and the Monotone Filtration ℚ ⊆ deg≤1 ⊆ deg≤2 ⊆ ...
content:
Section 5 establishes two structural facts about the degree stratification:

**`rat_algebraic_degree_one`**: Every rational q ∈ ℚ is algebraic of degree 1:
```lean
theorem rat_algebraic_degree_one (q : ℚ) :
    IsAlgebraic ℚ (algebraMap ℚ ℝ q) := isAlgebraic_algebraMap q
```
The proof is a single call to `isAlgebraic_algebraMap`, which states that any element mapped from the coefficient ring R into an R-algebra E via `algebraMap` is algebraic over R. For q ∈ ℚ mapped to ℝ, the minimal polynomial is X - q (degree 1), confirming degree exactly 1. This pins the bottom stratum: deg-1 ⊇ image(ℚ → ℝ).

**`bounded_degree_monotone`**: The degree-bounded sets form a monotone chain:
```lean
theorem bounded_degree_monotone (d : ℕ) :
    algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d ⊆ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree (d + 1)
```
Proof: if natDegree(minpoly x) ≤ d, then also ≤ d+1 by `Nat.le_succ_of_le`. This single-line proof establishes the filtration structure: the bounded-degree sets are nested ⋯ ⊆ B_d ⊆ B_{d+1} ⊆ ⋯ with exhaustive union (proved in §7). 

Together, these give the chain: ℚ ≅ algebraicRealsOfDegree 1 ⊆ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree 1 ⊆ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree 2 ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ all algebraic, with each inclusion proper (e.g., ∛2 ∈ B_3 \ B_2) and all having the same cardinality ℵ₀.
mathContext: `isAlgebraic_algebraMap` is the Mathlib lemma: for any `Algebra R E`, `∀ r : R, IsAlgebraic R (algebraMap R E r)`. It works because r satisfies the polynomial X - algebraMap r, which has degree 1 and coefficient 1 ≠ 0. This is the cleanest way to connect ℚ-rationality to degree-1 algebraicity in Lean.

title: Cardinal Paradox: Algebraic ≅ ℚ ≅ ℕ Despite Proper Containment ℕ ⊊ ℚ ⊊ Algebraic
content:
The theorem `card_algebraic_eq_card_rat` proves:
Cardinal.mk {x : ℝ // IsAlgebraic ℚ x} = Cardinal.mk ℚ

Proof:
```lean
rw [card_algebraic_reals_eq_aleph0, Cardinal.mk_denumerable]
```

Both sides equal ℵ₀: the left by `card_algebraic_reals_eq_aleph0`, the right because ℚ is Denumerable (has an explicit bijection to ℕ), giving `Cardinal.mk ℚ = Cardinal.aleph0` via `mk_denumerable`.

Similarly `card_algebraic_eq_card_nat` gives |algebraic reals| = |ℕ|.

This formalizes the 'Hilbert Hotel' phenomenon for algebraic numbers: adding √2, √3, ∛2, and all other algebraic irrationals to ℚ doesn't change the cardinality. The proper containment ℕ ⊊ ℤ ⊊ ℚ ⊊ algebraic reals is real (no surjection in the other direction), but all these sets have the same infinite cardinality ℵ₀.

The logical structure: |algebraic| = ℵ₀ = |ℕ| = |ℤ| = |ℚ| ≠ |ℝ| = 2^ℵ₀ = |ℂ| = |transcendentals|.

**Why this is the conceptual core of Cantor's 1874 theorem.** Cantor's December 1873 letter to Dedekind, and the resulting paper *Über eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen* (Crelle 77, 1874), introduces *two* theorems sequentially: (i) the algebraic numbers are countable; (ii) the real numbers are uncountable. The 1874 paper does *not* yet have the diagonal argument (that came in 1891); the 1874 uncountability proof uses the nested-intervals argument. The *combination* (i) + (ii) yields Cantor's first existence proof of transcendental numbers: since $|\overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = \aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0} = |\mathbb{R}|$, the set $\mathbb{R} \setminus \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of *transcendental* reals is non-empty — in fact has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (uncountably many transcendentals, only countably many algebraic). **This existence proof is non-constructive**: it certifies transcendentals exist without exhibiting any specific one. Liouville's 1844 explicit construction $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 10^{-n!} = 0.110001000…$ predated Cantor by 30 years and *did* exhibit specific transcendentals, but Cantor's cardinality argument established a far stronger conclusion: transcendentals are the *overwhelming majority* of real numbers in a precise cardinal-arithmetic sense.

**The density paradox: countable but topologically everywhere.** Despite their countability, the algebraic reals are *dense* in $\mathbb{R}$ — every open interval contains infinitely many algebraic numbers (in fact, infinitely many rationals, which are degree-1 algebraic). So $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{R}$ is a *countable dense subset* of $\mathbb{R}$, mirroring $\mathbb{Q}$'s topological behavior. The complement $\mathbb{R} \setminus \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (the transcendentals) is *also* dense — a meager-in-the-Baire-sense (uncountably many) set sandwiching a meager (countable) set. This is the same phenomenon as $\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \sqcup (\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q})$ where both halves are dense; here it's lifted from the $\mathbb{Q}$/irrational split to the $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$/transcendental split, with the *transcendental* irrationals as the genuinely-large complementary set.

**Cardinal-arithmetic strength of ℵ₀ + Hilbert Hotel intuition.** The Hilbert Hotel (Hilbert's lecture, c. 1924) captures the surprise: a hotel with rooms 1, 2, 3, … fully occupied can still accommodate an extra guest (move occupant $n$ to room $n+1$) — or accommodate a *countably infinite bus* of new arrivals (move occupant $n$ to room $2n$, freeing all odd rooms) — because $\aleph_0 + 1 = \aleph_0 + \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$. The 'algebraic = rational + algebraic irrational' equation here is the *infinite-bus version*: each irreducible polynomial of degree $\geq 2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ contributes at most $\deg(p)$ new algebraic numbers to the rationals, and the countable union $\bigcup_d \bigcup_{p : \text{degree } d} \text{roots}(p)$ remains countable by the cardinal identity $\aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$ (countable degrees, countably many polynomials per degree, finitely many roots per polynomial). The `iUnion_bounded` lemma (annotation `ann-algebraic-iUnion-bounded`) is the technical realization of this triple countable union.

**Connection to the continuum hypothesis (CH).** Cantor's 1874 paper is the *birth* of the cardinal hierarchy $\aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0}$, and the question 'is there an intermediate cardinal $\aleph_0 < \kappa < 2^{\aleph_0}$?' is precisely the *continuum hypothesis* he formulated in 1878. Cardinality of algebraic numbers fixes one end of the comparison: $|\overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = \aleph_0$ is *exactly* the lower bound, and any countable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ inherits this cardinality. By Gödel (1940, $\text{Con(ZFC)} \Rightarrow \text{Con(ZFC + CH)}$) and Cohen (1963, $\text{Con(ZFC)} \Rightarrow \text{Con(ZFC + }\neg\text{CH)}$), CH is *independent* of ZFC. The Lean formalization here cannot decide CH — it lives in the cardinal arithmetic Lean inherits from ZFC, where $2^{\aleph_0}$ remains opaque — but the inequality $|\overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = \aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0}$ is provable from ZFC alone (Cantor's diagonal theorem), and this file formalizes the $\aleph_0$ side of it. The transcendental-existence corollary follows from any model of ZFC, independently of how CH is decided in that model.

**Pedagogical placement.** This annotation is *the* result that conveys why Cantor's theorem matters — not just 'algebraic numbers are countable as a curiosity' but 'algebraic numbers are countable, transcendentals exist, the continuum is strictly larger than any explicitly-constructible number system'. The gallery cross-references `cantors-theorem` (uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$, the matching upper bound) and `liouville-theorem` (explicit transcendental construction) form the complete triangle with this entry; all three together establish the existence and abundance of transcendentals from independent angles — cardinality (Cantor 1874), diophantine approximation (Liouville 1844), and transcendence proofs for specific numbers like $e$ (Hermite 1873) and $\pi$ (Lindemann 1882) that the gallery formalizes in `hermite-lindemann`.
mathContext: Cardinal.mk_denumerable states: for any type α with [Denumerable α], Cardinal.mk α = Cardinal.aleph0. A type is Denumerable if it has a bijection to ℕ. ℚ is Denumerable (proved via the Cantor pairing function on ℤ × ℕ). This gives the cardinality equality without constructing an explicit bijection between algebraic reals and ℚ.
relatedConcepts: ℵ₀ arithmetic (ℵ₀ + n = ℵ₀, ℵ₀ · ℵ₀ = ℵ₀)
topological density of countable sets in ℝ
prerequisites: concept of constructive vs non-constructive existence proof

title: Exhaustive Filtration: algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_bounded Closes the Loop
content:
`algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_bounded` proves:
{x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} = ⋃ d : ℕ, algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d

This is the bounded-degree analogue of `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree` (§4). The proof mirrors the exact-degree version:
```lean
ext x; simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_iUnion, algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree]
constructor
· intro hx
  exact ⟨(minpoly ℚ x).natDegree, hx, le_refl _⟩
· rintro ⟨d, hx, -⟩
  exact hx
```
The key difference from the exact-degree version: the witness is d = natDegree(minpoly ℚ x), and the degree bound is `le_refl _` (natDegree ≤ natDegree) rather than `rfl` (natDegree = natDegree). This is a minor change but correctly matches the `≤` vs `=` distinction in the two set definitions.

Together with `bounded_degree_monotone` (§5), this closes the loop: the monotone chain B_0 ⊆ B_1 ⊆ B_2 ⊆ ⋯ exhausts all algebraic numbers. The section ends with `end AlgebraicNumbersCountable`, closing the namespace opened at line 68.
mathContext: The two union theorems — exact-degree and bounded-degree — are related by: ⋃ d, algebraicRealsOfDegree d = ⋃ d, algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d (both equal the algebraic reals). This is consistent because algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d = ⋃_{k=0}^{d} algebraicRealsOfDegree k, so the two unions have the same limit. The bounded-degree filtration is coarser (each B_d contains multiple exact strata) but has nicer topological properties.
